newsitem.title: UK: Ireland's PM hails ceasefire, urges real talks.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's PM hails ceasefire, urges real talks.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern said on Saturday that the new IRA truce presented a chance to build "a durable and balanced settlement" to the 28-year Northern Ireland conflict.

Ahern told Sky News that the Irish Republican Armys ceasefire in its war against British rule of Northern Ireland was an acknowledgement that violence could not bring about its goal of a united Ireland.
"No positive (Irish) republican ideal or any other ideal can be realised except by democratic means," Ahern told Sky by telephone.
Ahern's government is co-sponsor with Britain of Northern Ireland peace talks to which the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing can be admitted if its truce is deemed real by Britain.
"I welcome the speedy confirmation that the ceasefire has been unequivocally restored. I know that it's the beginning of another phase of work for us," he said.
Ahern said he understood scepticism among Northern Ireland's 1.5 million people about the sincerity of the IRA truce after the guerrillas broke a 17-month ceasefire in February last year.
"I understand those reservations because people who have borne the brunt of IRA attacks aover the years will of course always have reservations about this. That's totally understandable," he said.
Under new terms worked out by Britain and Ireland which persuaded the IRA to call its truce, guerrillas will not have to disarm as a condition for entry to the negotiations.
Ahern said he understood that people might be sceptical about IRA intentions if they remained armed while Sinn Fein negotiated.
"There are people this morning who will say I don't believe an inch of that," Ahern said.
"But isn't the absence of violence far better than listening to news of people being shot in their beds and people being blown up,? he said.
Ahern, whose country's constitution claims Northern Ireland and its people as Ireland's, said he looked forward to the talks process resuming in September to discuss substantive issues.
The negotiations have been bogged down for a year over proposals to disarm the guerrillas and the latest Anglo-Irish proposals on so-called parallell decommissioning will be voted on next Wednesday.
"The politcal solution and resolution of the conflict is still there to work on. But if we can try and do that with violence not involved then it wil be easier", he said.
